draft.title: Demand
card: Demand is how much of a product buyers want and can afford at each price. Wanting something is not enough. A buyer must also be able to pay for it.
As the price of a product rises, people usually buy less of it. As the price falls, they usually buy more.
Buyers cut back when prices rise for two reasons. Some cannot afford it any more, and some switch to a cheaper product instead.
A demand schedule is a table that lists the quantity buyers would purchase at each price. A demand curve is a line that shows the same thing on a graph, and it slopes down.

4.alt: A demand curve drawn from a demand schedule. At $5 buyers want 10, at $4 they want 20, at $3 they want 30, at $2 they want 40 and at $1 they want 50. The line slopes down: a higher price means fewer are bought.

draft.remember: Demand links price to the amount people buy: a higher price usually means less is bought.

a.q: A shop in Geelong cuts the price of its sandwiches. What usually happens to the number of sandwiches people want to buy?
opts: It goes up for wealthy buyers alone
a.why: As price falls, people usually buy more. A lower price puts the sandwiches within reach of more buyers, and some switch from other lunches. The effect is not limited to wealthy buyers.
a.clue: Think about what a lower price does to what buyers can afford.

b.q: Mia in Bendigo really wants a new phone that costs $900, but she has only $300 saved. Is she part of the demand for that phone at $900?
opts: No, as she cannot pay that price now
Yes, as she wants the phone very much
No, as she has not been to a shop yet
Yes, as she could save the rest later
b.why: Demand needs buyers who both want a product and can afford it at that price. Mia wants the phone but cannot pay $900, so she is not part of demand at that price. Wanting it a lot, or saving later, does not change what she can pay now.
b.clue: Demand needs more than wanting a product.

b.best: No, as she cannot pay that price now
